findings.title: Indexing-slicing on `events[last_assistant_idx..]` with `unwrap_or(0)`
findings.description: `events[last_assistant_idx..]` panics if `last_assistant_idx > events.len()`. Currently safe because `rposition()` guarantees a valid index and `unwrap_or(0)` is bounded by `events.len()`, but the pattern is fragile to refactoring (e.g. switching `unwrap_or(0)` to `unwrap_or(events.len())` would silently break). The consecutive-failure watchdog in `run()` walks the tail from the last assistant turn to count errors; an off-by-one here would either under-count (false-clean turns) or over-count.
findings.trigger: If the events slice is empty or the watchdog logic is changed to compute the index differently, the slice could panic in production.
findings.current_code:
let last_assistant_idx = events
    .iter()
    .rposition(|r| matches!(r.event, SessionEvent::AssistantMessage { .. }))
    .unwrap_or(0);
let errors = events[last_assistant_idx..]
    .iter()
    .filter(|r| matches!(r.event, SessionEvent::ToolError { .. }))
    .count();
findings.suggested_fix: Use `events.get(last_assistant_idx..).unwrap_or(&[])` or extract a helper that returns the slice and bounds-checks internally.

findings.title: Indexing-slicing on `Value` via `block["thought_signature"]`
findings.description: `serde_json::Value`'s `Index` impl panics if the value is not an Object. Currently safe because `json!({...})` always produces an Object, but any future change that lets `block` come from a non-Object source (e.g. parsing external JSON, JSON Merge Patch) would crash the tool_use serializer in the wire-encoding path. The harness serializes every assistant message's tool_use blocks; a panic here would propagate through the session log.
findings.trigger: If `tool_use_blocks` is ever called with `call.thought_signature` data that round-trips through a JSON Merge or a different macro path that may produce non-Object values.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `block.as_object_mut().expect("tool_use block is an Object").insert("thought_signature".into(), Value::String(sig.clone()));` or use `serde_json::Map::insert` on the underlying map.

findings.title: Repeated indexing-slicing in act_parallel pass — clippy noise but indicates missing Vec<&T> pattern
findings.description: 17 indexing-slicing findings all use `vec_name[idx]` where `idx` comes from `enumerate()` or a captured-at-dispatch index. Currently safe, but the pattern (`canonical_args[idx]`, `sanitized[idx]`, `blocked[idx]`, `skip[idx]`, `started_at[idx]`, `&tool_calls[idx]`) is everywhere — any mistake in index arithmetic would silently corrupt the wrong tool call. The parallel path stores parallel vectors keyed by position; a `Vec<Slot>` would be safer (compiler-enforced index validity) and remove the warnings.
findings.trigger: A future refactor that, e.g., sorts or filters `tool_calls` between indexing the parallel vectors would silently target the wrong slot.
findings.suggested_fix: Introduce `struct ParallelSlot { call: NativeToolCall, started: Instant, canonical: String, sanitized: Option<Value>, blocked: bool, skipped: bool }` and use `Vec<ParallelSlot>`. Eliminates the parallel-array foot-gun and the 14 of 17 clippy findings in one move.

findings.title: Repeated indexing-slicing in prompt.rs — all safe via upstream clamp/enumerate
findings.description: Six findings (lines 106, 264, 276, 290, 304, 470) all involve `events[idx+1..]` or `events[tail_start..]` or `events[..upper]`. All are bounded by upstream clamping (`tail_start_index`, `before_idx.min(events.len())`) or `enumerate()` indices. The clippy lint is overly conservative here; the actual code is panic-free. Mention only because the pattern recurs enough that a `let slice = &events[tail_start..];` followed by `slice.get(...)` style might be cleaner.
findings.trigger: No current production trigger.
findings.suggested_fix: Accept the clippy lint per-line (`#[allow(clippy::indexing_slicing)]` on the function) once verified, or extract `pub(crate) fn slice_from(events: &[SessionEventRecord], start: usize) -> &[SessionEventRecord]` that bounds-checks internally.

findings.title: `fire_boundary_grace_turn` invoked inconsistently — three paths wrapped in `tokio::time::timeout`, three not
findings.description: In `run()`: the `StallTimeout` and `TurnTimeout` paths wrap `fire_boundary_grace_turn` in `tokio::time::timeout(GRACE_TIMEOUT_BUDGET, ...)`. The `ConsecutiveFailureCap`, `VerifierVeto`, and `MaxIterations` paths call it directly without the outer timeout. The grace turn itself has an internal `tokio::time::timeout(GRACE_TIMEOUT_BUDGET, ...)` wrapper inside `fire_boundary_grace_turn`, so the run() paths are functionally equivalent — but the inconsistency obscures the design and risks a future edit dropping one wrapper while leaving the other.
findings.trigger: Any future refactor that adds a new cap site needs to remember both layers.
findings.suggested_fix: Either (a) move the `tokio::time::timeout` wrapper into `fire_boundary_grace_turn` only and remove it from the two run() callers (the inner timeout already covers it), or (b) make the wrapping explicit at every call site via a helper `fn fire_grace_with_timeout(...)`.

findings.title: `canonical_json_string` silently dedupes all fail-to-serialize args to empty string
findings.description: `serde_json::to_string(&canon(value)).unwrap_or_default()` returns `""` when serialization fails (non-finite floats NaN/+inf/-inf). This signature is then used as the cross-batch dedup key in `record_failure` / `is_recent_failure`. If two distinct tool calls ever produce non-finite numeric args (rare but possible — `f64::NAN` in JSON is explicitly rejected by serde_json), the dedup treats them as duplicates, refusing the second call with a synthetic ToolError. The defensive `unwrap_or_default()` was added because tool args/results are documented to never contain non-finite floats — but if a custom tool ever emits one, the dedup silently groups them.
findings.trigger: Any tool that emits NaN/+inf/-inf in its argument `Value` will be deduped against all other such calls (and against every prior failure that also fell back to "").
findings.current_code: serde_json::to_string(&canon(value)).unwrap_or_default()
findings.suggested_fix: Either (a) return `Result<String, _>` from `canonical_json_string` and surface a HarnessError on failure (R10: don't silently mask tool-input failures), or (b) include a per-call UUID in the dedup key alongside the canonical JSON so that "" collisions are impossible.

findings.title: `TraceSink::on_trace` called synchronously inside async loop — blocking impl stalls the whole harness
findings.description: Every `emit()` call invokes `sink.on_trace(&event)` synchronously, inline with the async harness. The trait doc says "Implementations MUST NOT block", but this is enforced only by documentation — a non-conforming impl would block the entire async harness task. Per turn the harness fires 4-10+ trace events; even a 10ms blocking impl would dominate wall-clock time. The Gateway path uses `GatewayTraceSink` which forwards into an mpsc queue (so the sink itself is non-blocking), but a custom test sink or future sink could violate the contract.
findings.trigger: Any new TraceSink implementation that performs sync I/O (file write, syslog, blocking HTTP).
findings.suggested_fix: Change the trait to `async fn on_trace(&self, event: &LoopTraceEvent)` (or spawn the call as the harness already does for `tool_signal_sink` in `push_tool_invocation`). Adds an `await` to every emit but matches the existing safety property of the tool-signal sink path.

findings.title: `HarnessCallback` `&mut self` consumed by sync `std::sync::Mutex` inside async sink
findings.description: `CallbackSink` wraps `&mut dyn HarnessCallback` in a `std::sync::Mutex` to satisfy `DeltaSink::on_delta(&self, ...)`. The harness's `stream_llm_call` constructs this sink, hands it to the provider, and the provider's streaming loop calls `on_delta` synchronously one at a time. The doc says "The lock is effectively uncontended: the provider drives one delta at a time on a single task." If a future decorator stack adds parallel polling or the provider ever spawns a delta-emitter, the std::sync::Mutex would deadlock against any other task that also tries to call the callback (e.g. a parallel emitter). The poisoning-recovery (`unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())`) masks the panic.
findings.trigger: A future streaming provider that emits deltas from multiple tasks, or that holds a callback borrow across an await.
findings.suggested_fix: Document the single-task invariant more loudly, OR use a tokio::sync::Mutex if parallel emission is anticipated, OR change `DeltaSink::on_delta` to take `&mut self` and refactor the harness to pass `&mut callback` to the streaming call. The current `std::sync::Mutex<&mut dyn HarnessCallback>` is unusual and warrants a clear contract.

findings.title: `tokio::time::Instant::from_std(started) + budget` — overflow risk with very long budgets
findings.description: `race_llm_call` constructs `tokio::time::Instant::from_std(started) + budget`. If `budget` (the `turn_timeout`) is so large that `started + budget` overflows `Instant`'s representation, the future either panics or behaves unpredictably (tokio uses saturating arithmetic internally but the contract is not documented). With `Some(Duration::from_secs(u64::MAX))` this would overflow; practical configs use 5 minutes so it's safe today, but the value flows from user config without validation.
findings.trigger: A misconfigured `turn_timeout` (e.g. accidentally set to seconds-instead-of-milliseconds and never validated) could overflow.
findings.suggested_fix: Use `tokio::time::sleep(budget)` (relative) instead of `sleep_until(started + budget)` — equivalent semantics, no overflow risk, and clearer intent. The `started` argument to `race_llm_call` could then be dropped from this branch (only used for the StalledTurn `elapsed` reporting).

findings.title: `#[allow(async_fn_in_trait)]` without stated reason
findings.description: The test-only extension trait `AgentHarnessTestExt` declares `async fn run_turn` and suppresses `async_fn_in_trait` without a `reason = "..."` justification. The lint flags this because the suppression is silent — a future reader has no way to tell whether the allow is load-bearing (e.g. the trait is `dyn`-used elsewhere) or cosmetic (single test impl). The trait has zero production callers and exactly one impl.
findings.trigger: A future reader/editor may mistake the suppression for permission to add `dyn`-bound calls, which `async_fn_in_trait` would break.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace with `#[allow(async_fn_in_trait, reason = "test-only trait with one impl; never used as dyn")]` so the suppression carries the design intent. Same change should be applied to the existing `#[async_trait::async_trait]` macro use if `dyn DeltaSink` is not needed.

findings.title: `AgentHarness::run` — 469 lines, cyclomatic 40, cognitive 104
findings.description: The outer run loop inlines: cap detection (stall, turn timeout, consecutive-failure, verifier-veto, max-iterations), follow-up continuation handling, session-split rebinding, watermark reset, and final trace event emission. Each cap site duplicates the `tokio::time::timeout(GRACE_TIMEOUT_BUDGET, fire_boundary_grace_turn(...))` + `break Ok(HitLimit)` pattern. Extracting per-cap handlers would dramatically reduce complexity and make adding a new cap a localized change.
findings.trigger: Maintenance burden when adding a new cap site or debugging a missed one; cognitive overhead reading the run loop.
findings.suggested_fix: Extract `fn handle_cap(&self, kind: CapKind, session, callback, iterations, cancel) -> LoopTraceSessionOutcome` that encapsulates the grace-turn + terminate_reason + trace-emit pattern. The outer loop becomes a clean match on cap kind.

findings.title: `AgentHarness::run_turn_internal` — 805 lines, cyclomatic 70
findings.description: The Think turn driver combines: event fetch, prompt assembly, recall injection, preflight cheap passes, budget evaluation, compaction directive, max-steps hint injection, request payload build, streaming gate evaluation, primary LLM call, reactive rescue, empty-response retry, max-tokens recovery loop, post-rescue drain, exit-point verdict capture, text-tool promotion, token accounting, output guardrail, streaming-vs-once emit suppression, tool-use promotion, verifier dispatch, verdict handlers (Halt / Veto / Done / Continue), and trace emission. Splitting into per-stage free functions (matching the existing `build_prompt_with_transient_tail` pattern) would dramatically improve readability.
findings.trigger: Maintenance burden when modifying any one stage (the rescue flow has already been split into helpers but still consumes 200+ lines inline).
findings.suggested_fix: Extract `async fn assemble_request(...)`, `async fn issue_llm_with_recovery(...)`, `async fn apply_output_guardrail(...)`, `fn handle_verdict(...)`. Keep `run_turn_internal` as a 50-line orchestrator that calls each stage.

findings.title: `AgentHarness::dispatch_group` — 331 lines, cyclomatic 27
findings.description: The serial-path body combines: offered-tool snapshot, steer checkpoint, per-call name repair, trace emit, request emit, tool-call guardrail, cross-batch dedup, within-batch memo, per-call cancel token, in-flight registration, ambient call identity, tool execution, post-exec budget apply, success/error result handling, timeline push, activity record. The `persist_tool_success` / `persist_tool_error` helpers already exist; extracting `execute_one_tool_call` for the in-loop body would simplify both this function and the parallel path.
findings.trigger: Maintenance when adding a new pre/post-dispatch step.
findings.suggested_fix: Extract `async fn execute_one_tool_call(&self, call, ..., guardrailed_args, parallel: bool) -> ExecOutcome`. The serial loop and the parallel PASS 0+1 would both become ~30 lines.

findings.title: `AgentHarness::act_parallel` — 303 lines, cyclomatic 25
findings.description: Three explicit passes (PASS 0 sequential prep, PASS 1 parallel dispatch, PASS 2 sequential transcript) total 300 lines inline. The PASS 0 loop alone is ~110 lines, mirroring the serial path's per-call body. Extracting `prep_call(idx, call, started_at, ...)`, `dispatch_live_futs(live_futs, parallelism)`, `record_completion(idx, outcome, ...)` would split the function into named stages.
findings.trigger: Maintenance when modifying the parallel fast path or adding a new per-pass step.
findings.suggested_fix: Extract `fn prep_call(...)`, `async fn dispatch_live_futs(...)`, `async fn record_completion(...)`. The main function becomes a clean three-stage pipeline.

findings.title: `build_prompt_with_transient_tail` — 276 lines, cyclomatic 28
findings.description: Prompt assembly is one big for-loop with a 6-arm match on `SessionEvent`, plus the trailing nudge injections (attempt_summary, no_progress, gather_budget, redundant_calls). The 6-arm match could be a method-dispatch table (`emit_event` per variant) and the four nudges could be a `Vec<fn(&[SessionEventRecord]) -> Option<UnifiedMessage>>` driven in a loop.
findings.trigger: Adding a new nudge type or a new SessionEvent variant requires editing this function.
findings.suggested_fix: Extract `fn emit_event(...)` for each variant; collect nudges into a `&[RenderNudge]` slice iterated post-loop.

findings.title: Whole-file oversized units — agent.rs (1017), act.rs (1269), prompt.rs (1375), think.rs (1662)
findings.description: Four files exceed 1000 lines. think.rs (1662) and act.rs (1269) each contain multiple `impl AgentHarness` blocks; splitting by concern (e.g. `harness/agent/think/{llm,verifier,recovery}.rs`) would localize changes. The harness's existing submodule layout (`agent/{act,prompt,think,guardrails}.rs`) is fine for the current split, but each module is itself large enough that further splitting would help.
findings.trigger: Cognitive load during review and editing.

src/harness/agent/act.rs:  1269 lines, single 577-line impl block.
src/harness/agent/prompt.rs: 1375 lines, 880-line test module.

findings.suggested_fix: Split think.rs into `think/{llm_call,recovery,verdict,grace}.rs` and prompt.rs test module into `prompt/tests.rs`. The act.rs impl already has natural sub-impls separated by comment headers; formalize as submodules.

findings.title: `can_parallel_dispatch` is `async` with no await — clippy `unused_async`
findings.description: `async fn can_parallel_dispatch` contains no `.await`. The function only performs synchronous checks (parallelism config, duplicate scan, `batch_parallelizable`). The `async` marker is unnecessary and forces every caller (one site) to write `.await`. Likely kept for trait-uniformity or future async claim queries.
findings.trigger: Confusion for readers; cargo clippy warning in CI.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove `async` (and the `.await` in the single caller). If async claim queries are anticipated, add `#[allow(clippy::unused_async, reason = "reserved for future async claim queries")]` and a TODO.

findings.title: `fire_boundary_grace_turn` re-reads full event log + rebuilds prompt for every cap site
findings.description: The grace turn function is 169 lines and re-fetches the full event log, runs `tail_start_index`, calls the input-guardrail `redact_session_input`, then calls `build_prompt`. The run loop's outer cap path can fire this turn from 5 different cap sites (stall, turn-timeout, consecutive-failure, verifier-veto, max-iterations) — and the function is async + LLM-bound. The work is necessary, but the function being in `think.rs` (a file already 1662 lines) means the function is hard to find and the redundancy of the LLM round-trip is hidden. Each cap site pays the cost of (a) full event fetch, (b) guardrail screening, (c) prompt rebuild, (d) one LLM call. For long sessions this can be 100ms+ of pure CPU before the LLM round-trip.
findings.trigger: Every capped run pays this cost; large sessions on slow disks may see noticeable grace-turn latency.
findings.suggested_fix: (a) Move `fire_boundary_grace_turn` to its own file `grace.rs` for discoverability. (b) Cache `last_assistant_has_text` and `tail_start_index` results when `run_turn_internal` already computed them — pass them in as args. (c) Consider a single-event-fetch path that only reads the tail (seq > last_prompt_seq) since the prompt builder already gets the full log fresh.

findings.title: `#[async_trait::async_trait]` on `RescueHost for AgentHarness` adds heap allocation
findings.description: Rust 1.75+ supports native `async fn` in traits (with RPITIT). The harness uses `#[async_trait::async_trait]` for both `DeltaSink` and `RescueHost`. For `RescueHost`, the trait is used only by the `context::compact::rescue` module which receives it as `&dyn RescueHost` — heap allocation per call. If `RescueHost` could be generic over the impl type (monomorphized at the rescue call site), the heap allocation disappears. `DeltaSink` is used via `dyn` trait object (passed to provider), so async_trait is needed there.
findings.trigger: Every reactive-compaction rescue pays one heap alloc per call for the dyn RescueHost.
findings.suggested_fix: If the rescue module can be made generic over `R: RescueHost`, drop async_trait. The doc comment already says the trait is "declared in the context layer and implemented here" — genericifying the context layer's API would remove the heap alloc without changing the trait shape.

This is a recurring macro-extraction opportunity — the duplicated bodies are nearly identical, suggesting they were hand-written rather than generated from a fixture builder.

findings.title: `agent.rs` `push_tool_invocation` spawns an unbounded detached task per tool call
findings.description: Every tool call (success or failure) triggers `tokio::spawn(async move { sink.record_tool_call(...).await })`. The harness never awaits these tasks. On a long run with thousands of tool calls, an unbounded number of detached tasks can pile up; a slow `RawMemoryToolSink` (the production wiring per deps.rs) could back-pressure the tokio runtime if the spawned tasks queue faster than the sink can drain. The doc claims "fire-and-forget" with the rationale "a slow store cannot back-pressure the harness loop" — true, but the unbounded spawn is itself a memory pressure risk.
findings.trigger: A long-running agent with thousands of tool calls on a slow disk-backed sink.
findings.suggested_fix: Either (a) use a bounded `mpsc` channel between the harness and the sink (the pattern already used by `GatewayTraceSink`), or (b) join on the spawn at end-of-turn (adds an `.await` to `act_parallel`'s PASS 2 and the serial loop's per-call site), or (c) document the spawn rate assumption and add a metric.
